manifest.label: Why I do this
manifest.title: I don’t bring a lecture to schools. I bring a project.
manifest.p1: Hi, I’m Denis. For eight years I taught computer science and physical education and worked in project-based learning. Today I’m deeply involved in AI, digital products, Unreal Engine and experiments where technology, education and society meet.
manifest.p2: For me, pedagogy isn’t a past profession but one of the pillars of my work. I’m interested in how people learn, what supports motivation, how to build an environment where people aren’t afraid to experiment, and how to connect play with real work. In my labs, students ask questions, try things out, create, verify and leave with an outcome that matters.

detail.contactTitle: Let’s turn {lab} into a project for your school.

ai-builder.question: From an idea to a working product
ai-builder.short: Prompts, context, Git, API, databases, deployment. We verify and explain what AI did.
ai-builder.lead: Students don’t just learn to write prompts. They come to understand the path from an idea to a working digital product. AI is not an authority here: it builds something, but students have to understand what happened, verify it, fix it and explain it.
studentsDo: They break an idea down into steps and work with prompts, tokens and context.
They use Git and GitHub, the CLI and APIs, and learn to manage API keys securely.
They store data in a database (e.g. Supabase) and try out both cloud and local models.
They deploy the app and explain what AI built in it and what they verified and fixed themselves.
ai-builder.output: A working, deployed app or tool, plus a short defence of their own solution.
ai-builder.tech: A computer classroom with internet access. We sort out accounts and API keys together, in line with the school’s rules and the students’ age.

unreal.question: The body, movement and digital worlds
unreal.short: Unreal Engine, Blueprints, Niagara, motion capture. The body and movement in a digital world.
unreal.lead: Unreal Engine as a space for gameplay, physics, animation, VFX, light and sound. Plus a second layer: body → movement → technology → digital space. Here technology doesn’t cut people off from their bodies; it helps them explore that relationship.
studentsDo: With help from AI, they build 3D environments and gameplay in Blueprints, tackling physics and camera work.
They work with materials, light, sound, animation and Niagara VFX.
They record their own movement with motion capture and transfer it onto a digital character.
They explore physical space, body awareness and the digital representation of people.
unreal.output: A playable scene or a short video from a digital world that also shows the students’ own movement.
unreal.tech: Computers with a dedicated graphics card, or shared workstations for teams. For motion capture, a camera and some open space are enough.

usage.question: What footprint does AI leave?
usage.short: Tokens, costs, privacy, digital value. We critically test an open hypothesis.
usage.lead: Every use of AI consumes resources, has a cost and has an impact. The lab is built on a real experimental project and an open question that students examine critically.
studentsDo: They measure the tokens, usage and costs of their AI queries and work with digital receipts.
They explore privacy, decentralisation, crypto and digital value.
They estimate environmental impact and compare where data comes from.
They test the hypothesis about benefits to society or nature, or reject it with reasoned arguments.
usage.output: A data study or infographic that uses arguments to support, question or refute the hypothesis.
usage.tech: A classroom with computers or laptops and an internet connection.

note.title: Open hypothesis
note.body: Could the value created by using technology form a new mechanism for supporting society or nature? It isn’t a settled truth. Students are free to reject it.

invok.question: How is an educational product made?
invok.short: A living case study of a real product: methodology, validation and dead ends.
invok.lead: Invok is a real educational product I’m working on. It serves as a living case study: how a product and its methodology take shape, AI literacy, UX, validation, feedback, rebranding and the dead ends too.
studentsDo: They follow how a real product takes shape, dead ends and rebranding included.
They design and test AI literacy activities and gather feedback.
They learn to validate an idea and make both product and pedagogical decisions.
They try out entrepreneurship on a real case, not a hypothetical scenario.
invok.output: A tested design for an activity or feature, with an argument for why it does or doesn’t have educational value.
invok.tech: Space for teamwork, flipcharts and, depending on the focus, a few laptops.

note.title: Fairness
note.body: Students are not free labour; the purpose of the lab is educational. If a student outcome ever grew into a real commercial collaboration, it would be handled separately, transparently and fairly.

future.question: What do we want technology to do?
future.short: AI, nature, privacy, digital minimalism. Disagreement is a legitimate outcome.
future.lead: The key question isn’t what technology can do, but what we want it to do. Disagreement is a legitimate educational outcome: if a student concludes they don’t want to use AI and can give sound reasons for it, that’s a success.
studentsDo: They explore the relationship between AI, people, nature, society, creativity and education.
They discuss privacy, automation, dependence on technology and digital minimalism.
They compare local and cloud technologies, as well as transhumanism and biophilic transhumanism.
They formulate and defend their own ethical stance, including disagreement.
future.output: A manifesto, podcast, exhibition or public debate for the whole school.
future.tech: A room where people can sit in a circle. No tech required.
